story.name: トウキョウ ひとりぐらし
story.title: The Festival on Our Street
story.line: ブーケが まちの おまつりに いきます
story.ja: 土曜の午後、窓の外で太鼓の音。いつもの通りがちょうちんと屋台でいっぱいになっていた。浴衣のチッチと、焼きそば、チョコバナナ、かき氷。神輿がやってきて、町内会のたいへいたに「担いでみなよ！」と言われ、ブーケも「わっしょい」とさけびながら2ブロック担ぐ。川のそばでは、コンビニのレムがおじさんの金魚すくいの屋台を手伝っていた。ポイがやぶれて「もう少しだったのに！」。でもレムがこっそり1匹くれて、金魚の名前はモチ。帰り道、浴衣姿のアリゲッティが「傘はまだ持ってて。あしたは雨よ」。

segments.en: On Saturday afternoon, Rosie heard drums. Not far away. Close. Right outside her window.
She looked down from the balcony. Her quiet little street had changed. There were paper lanterns on strings, and food stands all the way to the river.
Her phone buzzed. It was Nana, standing in the street below and waving, in a blue cotton robe called a yukata.
Surprise! It's the shrine festival! It's the biggest night of the year on your street. You've got to come down!
There's a festival? On my street? Nobody told me! Okay, count me in. Give me two minutes.
The street smelled like grilled corn and soy sauce. Kids ran past with masks on the backs of their heads. Old men sat fanning themselves.
Okay, here's the plan. We eat everything. Fried noodles first. Then chocolate bananas. Then shaved ice. Trust me.
They ate fried noodles from paper boats, standing up, and shared a chocolate banana with rainbow sprinkles.
Rosie ate her strawberry shaved ice much too fast and gave herself a brain freeze.
Then the drums got louder, and the crowd moved to the sides of the street. Here it came.
It was a small golden shrine on thick wooden poles, carried on the shoulders of about thirty people, all shouting together.
That's the mikoshi. It's like a shrine you can carry. People say the god of the shrine rides inside and gets a tour of the neighborhood.
In the front, shouting louder than anyone, was a big bear in a white headband. When he saw Rosie, he grinned and waved her over.
Hey! You're the new girl in Mr. Nook's building, right? I'm Teddy, from the neighborhood association. Come on, grab a pole! Give it a shot!
Me? Really? Are you sure? I don't know the words!
Easy. There's only one word. Wasshoi! You shout it, and you push. That's the whole thing. You got this!
So Rosie squeezed in under one of the poles, between a tall man and a tiny grandmother who was much stronger than she looked.
The pole was heavy on her shoulder. Everyone moved together, shouted together, and bounced the shrine up and down.
Wasshoi, wasshoi. She shouted until her voice cracked. She had no idea where they were going, and she didn't care.
After two blocks, her shoulder was sore, and she was laughing so hard she could barely breathe.
See? Now you're part of the neighborhood. Next year, you're carrying it the whole way. No excuses!
Near the river was a stand with a shallow pool full of little orange goldfish. Behind it, looking sleepy, was Sherb from the convenience store.
Oh, hey! It's the rice ball girl! My uncle runs this stand. Wanna try? You get a paper scoop. If you catch a fish, you keep it.
The scoop was just a thin circle of paper on a plastic handle. Rosie leaned over and chased one little fish into a corner, very carefully.
She lifted it. For one second, the fish was on the scoop. Then the paper tore, and it dropped back in with a tiny splash.
No! I almost had it! It was right there!
Yeah, everybody says that. Here, don't tell my uncle. You can have this one anyway. This little guy likes you. I can tell.
He handed her a small plastic bag of water. Inside, one little orange fish looked at her very seriously.
Hi, little guy. I'm going to call you Mochi. Welcome to the family. It's just the two of us, but it's a nice apartment.
On the way home, she ran into Gayle, back from her sister's, in a pale purple yukata.
Rosie held up the fish, and then she started to say sorry about the umbrella.
Oh, you got one! Wonderful. And thank you for watering my tomatoes. The umbrella? Hang on to it. It's going to rain tomorrow.
That night, Mochi swam around and around in a salad bowl on the counter. Rosie lay on the tatami, with a sore shoulder and a full stomach.
Through the open window, she could still hear the drums, far away now, and somebody, somewhere, still shouting wasshoi.

ph.trap: 数に入れて＝参加する、という意味
shot＝撃つ ではなく「ためし」
これを手に入れた ではなく、はげましの言葉
おこっているのではなく、明るく念をおしている
持っていた ではなく、あと一歩でできた
話せる ではなく、様子でわかる
ぶらさがる ではなく、手放さずに持っておく

predict.ask: つぎの はなしで、なにが おこる？
choices: Mochi the goldfish jumps out of the bowl and into the river.
A small earthquake shakes her apartment, and the next day there's a drill.
Teddy asks her to lead the festival next year.
predict.ja: 小さな地震で部屋がゆれ、次の日は防災訓練。
